newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Shell to manage offshore oil venture in Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Shell to manage offshore oil venture in Kazakhstan.

text.p: Shell Oil Co will manage a new operating company for an international consortium planning to develop Kazakhstan's vast offshore oil reserves, a company official said in an interview on Tuesday.
A production sharing agreement with the Kazakh government was also expected this summer, the official said.

"The foreign partners have set up a team to do this work and in the interests of efficiency, it should be staffed by one company," Richard Preston, Shell's venture manager for the KazakhstanKaspiyShelf (KCS) consortium, told Reuters. "That is Shell."

Consortium members have been coy about divulging details of likely reserves or production levels, but Preston said that KCS was possibly looking at peak production of up to one million barrels per day.
He said a joint-owned operating company managed by Shell, part of Anglo-Dutch oil giant Royal Dutch Shell, would be formed once an agreement was signed.
KCS was set up in 1993 to survey 100,000 square km of virgin acreage off the former Soviet republic's Caspian Sea coast, one of the largest offshore searches in the history of oil exploration.
The $300-million survey, to be wound down next month, was the consortium's entry ticket to first rights on Kazakhstan's rich offshore fields.
The KCS consortium comprises Shell, Agip SpA of Italy, British Gas Plc, an alliance of British Petroleum Co Plc and Norway's Statoil, Total SA of France and Mobil Corp of the United States.
Consortium members have let slip few details of talks on the production sharing agreement.
"Officially the target date (for signing) is the middle of the year -- there's no reason to believe it can't be concluded relatively quickly," said Preston.
He said confusion over the recent shake-up of Kazakhstan's state oil structures, replacing the oil and gas ministry with state-owned company Kazakh Oil, had not affected talks.
"It (the shake-up) was a concern, but it hasn't slowed things down -- we see the same faces around the negotiating table," Preston said.

Kazakhstan's offshore reserves have been the subject of much speculation after a Kazakh official said last year the area surveyed contained an estimated 10 billion tonnes of crude oil and two trillion cubic metres of natural gas.
Preston was cautious on oil reserves in the survey area.
"What you see in a seismic survey does not mean there is oil," said Preston.
"Russian data says there are many billions of barrels potentially, and we don't dispute that," Preston said.
He also pointed to tough challenges ahead in pumping and exporting the crude, including the need to drill to depths in excess of four km.
"Logistically it's complicated. It's in a nature reserve, it's in very shallow water so access is bad and it's a landlocked sea which is iced up in winter," Preston said.
KCS also has the problem over exports faced by all other oil majors looking to develop the Caspian basin's huge resources.
"It's a big issue, it's got to be for a landlocked country," said Preston. "The value is not how many barrels of oil you have under the surface, but how many barrels you have at the market."
He said the project's high output target would mean the consortium would build its own export pipeline.
He said large amounts of gas in the fields was also a major problem, with volumes too great to sell to the local market and expensive to deal with.
